lesson.title: Evidence and credence

steps.headline: Evidence moves a belief from a prior to a posterior.

lead.text: Your prior is how likely a hypothesis was before the evidence. Your posterior is how likely it is after.
Bayes' theorem links them: P(H | E) = P(E | H) × P(H) / P(E). Counting people gives the same answer more simply.
Picture the 1,000 people in two groups, the ill and the well. The test flags people in both.
Of everyone who is flagged, ask how many are ill.

reveal.text: You counted the positives from both groups. A positive result leaves a 50% chance of illness, far below the test's 90% hit rate.

steps.headline: A test catches 80% of cases and flags 5% of healthy people. 20% of 1,000 people have the condition. What share of positives are ill?

workedSteps.text: Count the positives in each group.
Divide the ill positives by all positives.

steps.headline: The same 90% hit rate and 10% false alarms, now on a condition that affects 1% of 1,000 people.

reveal.text: A positive result now means illness only 9 times in 108, about 8%. Judging a test by its hit rate while ignoring how rare the condition is, is called base-rate neglect.

workedSteps.text: Find how many people are ill, and how many of them the test catches.
Apply the false-alarm rate to everyone who is well, and add the two groups of positives.

lead.text: Bayes' theorem has an odds form: posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio. The likelihood ratio compares how probable the evidence is if H is true with how probable it is if H is false.

reveal.text: A 10% prior is odds of 1 to 9. Multiplying by the ratio gives even odds, which is 50%. A 1% prior is 1 to 99, and the same test lifts it only to 9 to 99.

lead.text: Change one number at a time and recount. Here the test is weaker at catching cases but gives fewer false alarms, and the condition affects one person in ten.

reveal.text: Lowering false alarms usually does more for a rare condition than raising the hit rate, because most positives then come from the healthy group.

lesson.orientation: Update a degree of belief with Bayes' theorem, using natural frequencies, base rates and likelihood ratios.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: In a town of 1,000 people, 100 have a condition. A test flags 90 of those 100. It also flags 90 of the 900 people who do not have it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll update a belief by counting people, and explain why a good test can mislead for a rare condition.
intro.whyItMatters: Medical tests, forecasts and news all hand you evidence. Counting is how you weigh it.

recap.keyIdea: Evidence does not settle a belief alone. How far a positive result moves you depends on how common the hypothesis was, so count both groups.

blocks.text: You counted 90 ill and 90 well people among the positives, saw the same test fall to about 8% when the condition was rare, and found the factor of 9.

recap.nextHook: Beliefs do not float free of the body. Next, Descartes on how mind and body relate.

questions.prompt: 1,000 people are screened. 10% have the condition. The test is positive for 90% of people with it and for 10% of people without it. What percentage of people who test positive have the condition?
hints: Find how many of the 1,000 have the condition, and how many of those test positive.
Find how many of the healthy people test positive.
Divide the ill positives by all positives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 are ill and 90 of them test positive. 900 are well and 90 of them test positive. 90 of 180 positives are ill: 50%.

questions.onCorrect: 50%. Half of the positives are ill, far below the test's hit rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the test's hit rate among the ill. The question asks what share of all positives are ill.
That is the false-alarm rate. Divide the ill positives by all positives.

questions.prompt: The same test (90% hit rate, 10% false alarms) is used on 1,000 people, of whom 1% have the condition. How many people test positive in total?
hints: Find the number who are ill, then the number of them the test catches.
Apply the false-alarm rate to everyone who is well.
Add the two groups of positives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 10 are ill and 9 test positive. 990 are well and 99 test positive. 9 + 99 = 108.

questions.onCorrect: 108 positives. A rare condition produces mostly false alarms, which are 99 of them.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the ill people the test catches. Add the healthy people it flags.
That counts only the false alarms. Add the ill people the test catches.

questions.prompt: A test is positive for 90% of people with a condition and for 10% of people without it. By what factor does a positive result multiply the odds that someone has the condition?
hints: The factor is the likelihood ratio.
Compare P(positive | condition) with P(positive | no condition).
Divide the hit rate by the false-alarm rate.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The likelihood ratio is 0.9 / 0.1 = 9, so posterior odds are nine times the prior odds.

questions.onCorrect: A factor of 9. The likelihood ratio is the hit rate divided by the false-alarm rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap between the two rates. The likelihood ratio compares them by dividing.

questions.prompt: Of 1,000 people, 10% have a condition. A test catches 80% of cases and is positive for 5% of people without the condition. What percentage of positives have the condition?
hints: Count the ill people the test catches.
Count the healthy people it flags.
Divide true positives by all positives and convert to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: 64%: 80 true positives out of 125 positives in all.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of true positives. Express it as a share of all positives.
That is the number of false alarms. Divide the true positives by all positives.

questions.prompt: P(H) = 0.2, P(E | H) = 0.5 and P(E | not-H) = 0.25. Find P(H | E), as a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Find the probability of E and H together.
Find the probability of E without H, using P(not-H) = 1 − P(H).
Divide the first by the sum of both.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The joint probability of E and H is 0.2 × 0.5 = 0.1; of E without H, 0.8 × 0.25 = 0.2. So P(H | E) = 0.1 / (0.1 + 0.2) = 1/3.

questions.onCorrect: A third: the ill positives divided by all positives, counted group by group.

misconceptions.feedback: That is P(E | H), the hit rate. Weigh it by how likely H was, then compare with the other route to E.
That is the joint probability of E and H. Divide it by the probability of E overall.

questions.prompt: What is the name for the error of judging P(H | E) from P(E | H) while ignoring how common H was to begin with? Two words are enough.
hints: The neglected quantity is the prior: how often H holds in the population.
Statisticians call that frequency the '___ rate'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Base-rate neglect, also called the base-rate fallacy.

questions.onCorrect: Base-rate neglect: ignoring how common the hypothesis was before the evidence.

misconceptions.feedback: Those describe the test. The neglected quantity is how common the condition was to begin with.

questions.prompt: How many people in the town test positive in all?
hints: The test flags people in two groups. How many in each?
One group is the 100 who have the condition. The other is the 900 who do not.
Add the people flagged in both groups.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 90 of the ill and 90 of the well are flagged: 90 + 90 = 180.

questions.onCorrect: 180 flags come from two groups. Counting both is the first step in weighing a test result.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts one group. The test flags people who are ill and people who are well.
That is how many have the condition. Count everyone who tests positive.

questions.prompt: A condition affects 1 person in 100. Before any test, what is your prior that you have it?
hints: The prior is set before the evidence arrives.

choices.label: The chance of a positive result

questions.onCorrect: The prior is the starting probability, here set by how common the condition is.

misconceptions.feedback: The hit rate describes the test. The prior is how likely the hypothesis was before testing.
A positive result is the evidence. The prior comes before it.

questions.prompt: Why divide by all the positives, not only the ill ones?
hints: Ask what group the question is about.

acceptedIdeas: The question asks what share of those who test positive are ill.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The question asks what share of those who test positive are ill.

choices.label: The question asks what share of those who test positive are ill.
The ill people are the majority.

questions.onCorrect: The posterior is about everyone who tests positive, so the false alarms belong in the total.

misconceptions.feedback: In this town the ill people are a minority. The reason lies in what the question asks.
False alarms are part of the positives. They change the answer.

questions.prompt: A test is positive for 90% of ill people and 10% of healthy ones. Half of 1,000 people are ill. What percentage of positives are ill?
hints: Split the 1,000 into ill and well, then count the flagged in each.
Find how many of the ill test positive, and how many of the well do.
Divide the ill positives by all positives and convert to a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 500 ill, of whom 450 test positive. 500 well, of whom 50 test positive. 450 ÷ 500 = 90%.

questions.onCorrect: Common conditions change the answer: with half the town ill, most positives are real.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the prior. Count how many ill people the test catches and how many healthy people it flags.
That is the false-alarm rate. Divide the ill positives by all positives.
